title: Simple Factory Pattern
oneLiner: Centralizes every 'new X()' call behind one function, hiding construction details without the full Factory Method subclass hierarchy.

hero.name: The Dispatcher
hero.catchphrase: One function, every type — say what you need, I'll hand you the class.
hero.power: Centralizes object construction behind one function, so callers never write 'new SpecificClass()' directly.
hero.weakness: Unlike Factory Method, it can't be extended by subclassing — adding a new type means editing the dispatcher's own code, not just adding a new file.
hero.origin: The Dispatcher appeared after `new StripeGateway()`, `new PaypalGateway()`, and `new RazorpayGateway()` calls were scattered across 40 different files, each needing to know every concrete gateway class.

story.problem: Forty different files each call `new StripeGateway()` or `new PaypalGateway()` directly, depending on which provider they need. Every file has to know every concrete gateway class that exists.
story.solution: The Dispatcher introduces one function, `createGateway(type)`, that hides every 'new' call behind a single switch. Callers just ask for a type by name.
story.result: Forty call sites shrink to `createGateway("stripe")`. No file outside the factory itself needs to know the concrete gateway classes exist.

before: Forty files each construct concrete classes directly
Every caller needs to know every concrete class
Construction logic is duplicated wherever a gateway is needed
after: One function centralizes every construction call
Callers only need to know a type name, not a concrete class
Construction logic exists in exactly one place

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A codebase search for 'new StripeGateway' returns 14 matches across 14 different files.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We renamed the Stripe class and now I have to update 14 files that all constructed it directly.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Dispatcher appears behind a single counter, taking requests and handing back the right class.
panels.speaker: The Dispatcher
panels.dialogue: Stop calling 'new' all over your codebase. Ask ME for what you need by name — I'll hand you the right instance.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: createGateway('stripe') hides the concrete class behind one function that every caller shares.
panels.speaker: The Dispatcher
panels.dialogue: Only I need to know the concrete classes exist. Every caller just says the type name and gets back a working gateway.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The 14 scattered call sites collapse into one function with one switch statement.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Renaming the Stripe class now means editing one file, not fourteen.

code.before:
// Scattered across dozens of files
const gateway = provider === "stripe" ? new StripeGateway() : new PaypalGateway();

useWhen: Multiple places in the codebase construct one of a known, small set of related classes.
You want to hide concrete class names from callers without building a full subclassed Factory Method hierarchy.
The set of types is relatively stable and doesn't need to be extended without touching the factory itself.
avoidWhen: There's only one type being constructed — there's nothing to centralize.
The set of types needs to be extended by third parties without modifying your factory's source — that calls for real Factory Method or a registry.
The construction logic per type is trivial enough that the factory function adds more indirection than value.
commonMistakes: Calling this 'the Factory pattern' and assuming it's the GoF Factory Method — Simple Factory isn't a formal GoF pattern, and doesn't support subclass-based extension the way Factory Method does.
Letting the switch statement grow unbounded instead of eventually graduating to Factory Method or a lookup registry once the type count gets large.
Leaking the concrete class back to the caller anyway (e.g. via casting), quietly defeating the point of centralizing construction.
Forgetting to handle the 'unknown type' case, letting an invalid input fail confusingly deep inside the factory.
explanation.realWorldExample: UI component factories (`createIcon(name)`), logging library factories that return the right logger implementation per environment, and most `create*()`-style helper functions found in everyday codebases are Simple Factory, whether labeled that way or not.

conversation.speaker: The Dispatcher
conversation.message: Close cousin, but simpler — and not actually a GoF pattern. Factory Method uses SUBCLASSES to let new creators be added without touching existing code. I'm one function with a switch — extending me means editing my own source.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So when do I graduate from you to real Factory Method?

conversation.speaker: The Dispatcher
conversation.message: When outside code needs to plug in NEW types without ever touching my source file. That's exactly the extension point Factory Method gives you, and I don't.

codeBattle.scenario: Your app constructs one of three known logger implementations (console, file, remote) in about a dozen places, and you just want one place that hides which concrete logger class gets built.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Dispatcher is exactly right for a small, stable set of known types where you just want one function centralizing construction — no subclass hierarchy needed.

quiz.question: Is Simple Factory one of the 23 official Gang of Four patterns?
options: No — it's a widely-used idiom, but not a formal GoF pattern
Yes — it's the first pattern in the Creational category
Yes — it's the same as Abstract Factory
No — it doesn't actually exist in real codebases
quiz.answer: No — it's a widely-used idiom, but not a formal GoF pattern
quiz.explanation: Simple Factory is an extremely common construction idiom, but the GoF book's actual Creational patterns are Factory Method and Abstract Factory.

quiz.question: How does Simple Factory typically decide which concrete class to construct?
options: A single function uses a switch or lookup on a type parameter
Each concrete class is a subclass overriding a shared creation method
It always returns a Singleton instance
It reads the type from a database at compile time
quiz.answer: A single function uses a switch or lookup on a type parameter
quiz.explanation: The defining trait of Simple Factory is exactly this: one function branching on a type value to decide what to construct.

quiz.question: What's the main structural limitation of Simple Factory compared to Factory Method?
options: Adding a new type requires editing the factory's own source, rather than adding a new subclass
It can only ever construct one type of object
It cannot be called more than once
It requires inheritance to work at all
quiz.answer: Adding a new type requires editing the factory's own source, rather than adding a new subclass
quiz.explanation: Factory Method's subclass-based extension point is exactly what Simple Factory trades away for simplicity.

quiz.question: When should you consider graduating from Simple Factory to real Factory Method?
options: When outside code needs to add new types without modifying the factory's own source
When you only ever have one type to construct
When performance is the only concern
When you want to remove all construction logic entirely
quiz.answer: When outside code needs to add new types without modifying the factory's own source
quiz.explanation: That open-for-extension property is exactly what formal Factory Method provides via subclassing.
